lessons.title: Welcome to BuildAndDo
lessons.summary: Learn the Observe → Understand → Act → Verify loop and read workspace state without mistaking a plan for a result.
lessons.prerequisites: None — start here.

outcomes: Identify the four parts of the work loop.
Distinguish missing data from a failed data request.
lesson.why: A shared workspace is useful only when people can tell an observation, a proposal and a verified result apart. This habit prevents an attractive dashboard from becoming a substitute for evidence.
preparation: Open BuildAndDo; sign in only when saving an exercise.
Use a test workspace you are allowed to change.

sections.heading: Understand the idea
paragraphs: BuildAndDo asks you to keep four things apart that most tools blur together. OBSERVE is recording what a source actually returned, in its own words. UNDERSTAND is saying what that observation might mean while keeping the uncertainty visible. ACT is performing one approved, bounded step. VERIFY is going back and inspecting whether the thing you did produced the outcome you claimed it would.

The loop matters because each stage can fail on its own and the failures look alike from a dashboard. A number on a card can mean 'we counted three' or 'we could not reach the thing that counts', and those are opposite situations. An empty list is a valid answer; an unavailable notice is the application telling you it does not currently know. Treating the second as the first is how a team ends up confident about a system it has stopped being able to see.

The same distinction applies to your own work. A mission saved as proposed is a sentence somebody wrote. It is not permission, it is not an attempt, and it is certainly not a result. Refreshing the page does not move it along. Every stage leaves its own record precisely so that nobody has to infer one from another.

sections.heading: Try it in BuildAndDo
steps: Open Overview and write down which workspace is active. If you cannot tell, that is your first observation.
Visit Signals and Evidence. For each, note the source and timestamp shown, or note that an explicit empty state is shown instead.
Open Missions and find one proposed item. Write down what would have to be true for it to be finished.
Find one number anywhere in the interface and answer: is this counted, or is it a default shown because something could not be read?
Write one observation you are confident in, and one question the interface cannot currently answer.

sections.heading: Worked example
paragraphs: A clinic notices missed appointments and someone proposes an SMS reminder. Walk the loop with real numbers rather than describing it.

OBSERVE: the booking export for March lists 240 appointments, 31 marked 'no-show'. The source is the export, dated 1 April. That is the observation - 31 rows with a flag, not 'we have a no-show problem'.

UNDERSTAND: 31 of 240 is 12.9%. It might be forgetting, it might be that Tuesday clinics run late and people give up, it might be that the flag is set by hand and someone has been thorough only recently. The uncertainty stays visible: we do not yet know why.
ACT: one bounded step - send reminders for one week, to one clinic, 24 hours ahead. The mission is approved before anything is sent, and the approval is its own record.

VERIFY: the following week's export shows 58 appointments, 4 no-shows, 6.9%. Two further records exist: 54 reminders were accepted by the SMS provider, and 2 failed with an invalid-number error. Note what this does NOT prove - one week, one clinic, and nothing rules out the weather. It is evidence, not a conclusion.

sections.heading: When this goes wrong
paragraphs: Here is the same work done badly, and it is worth recognising because it looks tidier than the version above.

Someone opens the dashboard, sees 'reminders: 54', and reports that reminders are working. The 54 is the count of messages the provider ACCEPTED. It is not the count delivered, not read, and not acted on. The two failures do not appear on the card at all. The team now believes something a receipt cannot support.

The tell is that no record was inspected between the claim and the number. A count on a card is a summary of rows somebody saved; it inherits every assumption those rows were saved under. If you cannot name the source and the timestamp, you are reading a dashboard, not evidence.

The repair is not more numbers. It is asking, of any figure you are about to repeat: what would this look like if the thing it measures had stopped working? If the answer is 'the same', the figure is not telling you anything.

exercise.prompt: Describe one small business problem using the four stages. Save real records only if you have permission.
checklist: Name the source of the observation.
Identify the approval needed before acting.
Specify an observable result.

check.question: A mission has been saved as proposed. What can you conclude?
choices: Its business outcome is verified.
A proposal was recorded; execution and outcome remain unproven.
The related service is installed.
check.explanation: A saved proposal proves that the plan exists. Later actions and evidence are separate observations.

lessons.legacy_summary: The Observe → Understand → Act → Verify loop, and how your workspace is organized.

lessons.title: Selecting and verifying a domain
lessons.summary: Separate a discovered domain, a selected target and permission to operate on it.
lessons.prerequisites: Read earlier lessons in this path; use an authorized test workspace for exercises.

outcomes: Describe selected versus verified domain state.
Record what ownership evidence is still missing.
lesson.why: A hostname is an address, not a grant of authority. Keeping ownership and verification separate helps you avoid running an otherwise reasonable task against the wrong organization.
preparation: Have a domain you control or use an explicitly labelled example.
Do not enter DNS credentials or verification secrets in notes.

sections.heading: Understand the idea
paragraphs: Choosing a domain in a form and controlling that domain are different facts, and the gap between them is where most launch problems live. SELECTED means you typed it and the application stored your intent. VERIFIED means something outside the application answered in a way only the owner could have arranged.

Nothing in a workspace can grant you authority over a name you do not own. The application can record that you intend to use example.com; it cannot make the registrar agree. Verification is always an OUTSIDE fact - a DNS record you were able to publish, a file served from a host you control, an email to an address in the registration. Those are things only an owner can do, which is exactly why they count.

Keep the evidence separate from the intent. 'We selected it on Tuesday' belongs in one record; 'the TXT record resolved at 14:20' belongs in another. When the two are merged into a single green tick, nobody can later answer the only question that matters: what did we check, and when?

sections.heading: Try it in BuildAndDo
steps: Open the workspace settings and find where a domain is named. Record its current state in the application's own words.
Ask what would have to be true outside BuildAndDo for that name to be yours. Write the specific check, not 'verify the domain'.
If a verification method is offered, read what it will actually test - a DNS record, a served file, an email - and note which one.
Write down the ownership evidence you do NOT have yet. This list is the honest state.
If you own a test domain, run one verification and record the timestamp and the value that was returned.

sections.heading: Worked example
paragraphs: A trades business wants buildandco.example for its booking page. Follow what each step does and does not establish.
They type the name into the workspace. State: SELECTED. What this establishes: one person's intent, stored. What it does not establish: anything at all about the registrar.

They are asked to publish a TXT record, _bnd-verify.buildandco.example, with a token. They add it at their DNS host. Twenty minutes later a lookup returns the token. State: VERIFIED, with the evidence being 'TXT lookup returned the expected token at 14:20 UTC'.

Notice what carried the weight. Not the form, not the twenty minutes, not anyone's confidence - the fact that only someone with DNS access could have put that token there. That is the whole mechanism.

Now the useful question: if the DNS record is deleted next month, what happens? The verification was true at 14:20 on that date and says nothing about today. A verification is a measurement with a timestamp, not a permanent property.

sections.heading: When this goes wrong
paragraphs: The common failure is quiet and takes weeks to surface.

Someone selects the domain, sees it listed in the workspace, and starts sending the address to customers. Nothing warns them, because selecting is a perfectly valid thing to have done. The application is not wrong; it recorded exactly what happened.

The break comes later: the certificate cannot be issued, or the mail bounces, and the state has been SELECTED the entire time. Everyone remembers 'adding the domain' and nobody can say who checked it, because nobody did. The record shows an intent that was read as an achievement.

Two habits prevent it. Say the state out loud when you report progress - 'selected, not yet verified' is four extra words. And when you see a domain listed anywhere, ask what outside fact was recorded against it. If the answer is nothing, it is a plan.

exercise.prompt: Write a domain-verification note with target, environment, authority source and missing evidence.
checklist: Spell the target hostname exactly.
Separate observed ownership from a pending check.
Exclude credentials and secret values.

check.question: Does selecting a domain authorize changes to its DNS?
choices: Yes, if the domain appears in search.
Yes, after adding it to a workspace.
No; ownership and the specific change authority must be established.
check.explanation: Selection is an organizational choice. Ownership verification and permission for the intended change are separate.

lessons.legacy_summary: How domain discovery works, what 'selected' vs 'verified' means, and why a found domain is not an authorized domain.

lessons.title: Reading the Signals feed
lessons.summary: Read observations, confidence and timestamps before turning a signal into work.
lessons.prerequisites: Read earlier lessons in this path; use an authorized test workspace for exercises.

outcomes: Separate a source fact from an interpretation.
Identify one useful follow-up check.
lesson.why: Signals compete for attention. Preserving source and freshness lets a team act on the strongest observation rather than the most dramatic wording.
preparation: Open Signals in an authorized workspace.
If there are no records, use the illustrative example without inventing a live event.

sections.heading: Understand the idea
paragraphs: A signal is a claim about the world with a source attached. The feed shows two very different kinds of thing side by side, and reading it well is almost entirely the skill of telling them apart.

An OBSERVATION is what a source returned: 'the checkout endpoint answered 500 on 14 requests between 09:10 and 09:40'. You can re-run it. Somebody else can get the same answer. An INFERENCE is what a person or an agent made of that: 'checkout is broken for mobile users'. That may well be right, but it is not the same kind of statement, and it cannot be re-run - it can only be argued with.

The reason the platform insists on the distinction is that inferences are more useful and more dangerous. They tell you what to do; they also carry whoever wrote them into your decision. A signal that cites its evidence lets you check the step from one to the other. A signal that does not is asking for trust, and the feed cannot tell you whether that trust is warranted.
Severity is a judgement too. 'High' means somebody decided it was high. Look for what the severity rests on before letting it set your order of work.

sections.heading: Try it in BuildAndDo
steps: Open Signals and pick any item. Read it once and decide: is this something a source returned, or something somebody concluded?
Find its source. If there is a link or an evidence reference, follow it and see whether it says what the signal says it says.
Write the signal's claim in your own words, then write the strongest alternative explanation for the same observation.
Check the type field. If it says inference, look for the evidence it cites. If it cites none, note that - a judgement with no grounds is still information, about the author.
Identify one follow-up check that would separate the signal's explanation from your alternative one. That check is more valuable than agreeing.

sections.heading: Worked example
paragraphs: A signal reads: 'Sign-ups have collapsed since the new pricing page shipped.' Severity high. Work through it rather than reacting to it.

What is the observation underneath? Following the evidence: daily sign-ups were 40-50 for three weeks, then 12, 9 and 11 for the three days after the deploy. That part is checkable and appears to hold.
What is the inference? That the pricing page caused it. The word 'since' is doing an enormous amount of work - it states a sequence and implies a cause.

Alternative explanations that fit the same numbers: the deploy also changed the sign-up form; a paid campaign ended that week; analytics broke and is undercounting; those three days are a public holiday.

The separating check: look at sign-ups measured by a DIFFERENT source, and look at whether the form still submits. Two minutes of that is worth more than an afternoon of discussion. If the second source also shows 11, the analytics explanation is gone. If the form errors on submit, the pricing page was never the story.

sections.heading: When this goes wrong
paragraphs: The failure mode is not believing a false signal. It is treating a true observation and a plausible inference as one statement.

In the example, the numbers were right. Everything that followed - rolling back the pricing page, a week of work, a difficult conversation with whoever shipped it - rested on the word 'since'. If the real cause was the form, the rollback changes nothing and the team has now also lost the pricing work.
It is worth noticing why this is hard to catch: the signal was not wrong in a way you could point at. It was two claims wearing one sentence, and only one of them had evidence.

A practical habit: when a signal makes you want to act, split it in half out loud. 'Sign-ups dropped from 45 to 11' - what is the source? 'Because of the pricing page' - what would be true if that were false? If the second question has no cheap answer, you are about to act on an interpretation.

exercise.prompt: Prepare a short signal assessment with one fact, two hypotheses and a next check.
checklist: Keep the source and observation time.
Use uncertainty language for explanations.
Define what new evidence would change your conclusion.

check.question: Which statement is an inference?
choices: The release caused the error spike.
The log contains three failed requests.
The observation was recorded at 09:00 UTC.
check.explanation: Causation requires additional evidence. A count or timestamp can be a direct observation when its source is recorded.

lessons.legacy_summary: Telling facts, inferences, and user-provided information apart, and what confidence means.

lessons.title: Proposing and approving a mission
lessons.summary: Build a bounded mission plan with explicit authorization, success criteria and review.
lessons.prerequisites: Read earlier lessons in this path; use an authorized test workspace for exercises.

outcomes: Save a useful mission draft.
Explain why approval is distinct from starting work.
lesson.why: A clear proposal makes the approver’s decision reviewable. The person authorizing work should know its scope, limits and recovery plan before anyone records work started.
preparation: Read a real signal or choose an illustrative business problem.
Identify an authorized approver; use demo mode for read-only exploration.

sections.heading: Understand the idea
paragraphs: A mission is how intent becomes something reviewable before it becomes something that happens. It moves through states, and each transition is a different person or a different moment being recorded: proposed, approved, running, and then verified or failed.

The gap between PROPOSED and APPROVED is the point of the whole mechanism. Proposing costs nothing and should be easy; anyone noticing a problem should be able to write it down. Approving is where somebody accepts that this is worth doing, in this scope, now. Collapsing the two - approving your own proposal the moment you write it - keeps the fields and loses the function.

RUNNING is not APPROVED either. Approval says the work may begin; running says it has. The distinction earns its keep when something goes wrong and you need to know whether anything was actually done.

A good mission plan answers questions a reviewer would otherwise have to ask: what is the smallest version of this, what would it look like if it failed, and how would we know. A plan that only describes success has not been thought about.

One more distinction earns its keep here: a mission that is DECLINED is a success of the process, not a failure of it. A reviewer who says 'not this sprint, and here is why' has produced something useful and reusable - the reason survives, and the next proposal can answer it. A process in which every proposal is approved is not a process that is going well; it is one where the approval step has stopped carrying information, and you will not be able to tell the difference by looking at the records.

sections.heading: Try it in BuildAndDo
steps: Open Missions and create a draft for something small and real in your test workspace.
Write the scope as what will be TRUE when it is done, not as a list of activities.
Write down what you expect to observe if it works - and separately, what you would observe if it silently did not.
Name who approves it and what they would need to see. If that is also you, say so - self-approval is a fact worth recording, not a thing to hide.
Save it as proposed and stop. Notice that nothing has happened yet, and that this is the correct state of the world.

sections.heading: Worked example
paragraphs: A workshop wants to stop losing quotes. Watch a vague mission become a reviewable one.
First draft: 'Improve the quoting process.' A reviewer cannot accept or decline this. There is nothing to disagree with, which feels like agreement and is not.

Second draft: 'Send a follow-up email 48 hours after any quote over £500 that has not been accepted, for the next two weeks, for the Bristol branch only.' Now it can be argued with - and that is the improvement.

The plan adds: baseline is 62 quotes last month, 18 accepted. Expected observation is the follow-up count and the acceptance rate for those specific quotes. Failure looks like emails sent with no change in acceptance, which is a real possible outcome and is written down in advance.

The approver asks one question the first draft could not have prompted: why £500? The answer - below that, the margin does not cover the follow-up - is the kind of thing that only surfaces when a proposal is specific enough to question.

sections.heading: When this goes wrong
paragraphs: The failure is not a rejected mission. It is a mission that was never really proposed.

Someone writes 'Improve the quoting process', approves it themselves, marks it running, and does some work. Every field is filled, every state transition is recorded, and the audit trail is complete. It is also empty: no scope was accepted because none was stated, and nobody could have declined because there was nothing specific to decline.
Six weeks later the question 'did that work?' has no answer. Not because the records are missing, but because the mission never said what would be different, so there is nothing to compare against.

The test to apply before approving anything, including your own: could a reasonable colleague read this and say no, for a specific reason? If not, it is not yet a proposal - it is an intention with a mission record wrapped around it.

Finally, notice what the states are FOR. They are not project-management decoration. Each one marks a point where a different question becomes answerable: was this worth doing (proposed to approved), did anyone start (approved to running), and did it do what it said (running to verified). If you find yourself unable to answer one of those about a piece of work, the missing answer usually corresponds exactly to a transition that was skipped.

exercise.prompt: Draft a mission that can be completed and checked in one short session.
checklist: State one measurable success criterion.
Name an explicit out-of-scope action.
Describe what happens if the check fails.

check.question: What should happen after materially changing an approved scope?
choices: Keep the old approval automatically.
Return the plan for approval of the new scope.
Mark the mission verified.
check.explanation: The new scope changes what was authorized. The saved approval must describe the work actually being performed.

lessons.legacy_summary: How a bounded mission is scoped, what you approve before anything runs, and how to review the plan.

lessons.title: Inspecting evidence and replay
lessons.summary: Use source-backed observations to review a mission without turning a receipt into a claim it cannot support.
lessons.prerequisites: Read earlier lessons in this path; use an authorized test workspace for exercises.

outcomes: Connect evidence to the correct mission and workspace.
Separate a recorded review from independent verification.
lesson.why: A receipt is valuable because someone else can inspect what happened. Evidence without a source or a clear connection to the claim makes reviews impossible to reproduce.
preparation: Use an existing test mission or inspect the example.
Remove customer information from learning artifacts.

sections.heading: Understand the idea
paragraphs: Evidence is the record of something that happened, kept so that a claim can be checked later by somebody who was not there. Its value comes almost entirely from two fields people skip: what the source was, and when it was taken.

A screenshot of a success message is evidence that a success message was shown. That is genuinely worth something and it is much less than it appears. It does not establish that an email arrived, that a payment settled, or that anyone read anything. The interface is reporting its own belief, and interfaces are frequently confident about things they have not checked.

The stronger form is a receipt from the far side: the provider's message id, the webhook that came back, a fetch of the thing you published returning what you published. The pattern to look for is whether the evidence was produced by the system that would know, or by the system that was hoping.

Replay matters for the same reason. Being able to re-run the observation and get the same answer separates a measurement from a memory. When you cannot replay, say so - 'measured once, on the 14th' is honest and useful; presenting it as a current fact is neither.

sections.heading: Try it in BuildAndDo
steps: Open Evidence and pick one record. Before reading its content, find its source and its timestamp.
Ask which system produced it: the one performing the action, or the one that would independently know the action landed?
Find which mission it belongs to. Evidence with no mission is an observation with nothing resting on it - note whether that is deliberate.
Try to re-run whatever produced it. If you can, compare the two answers. If you cannot, write down why not.
Write one sentence stating precisely what this record does and does not establish. That sentence is the skill.

sections.heading: Worked example
paragraphs: A mission claims a customer newsletter went out. Three records exist. They are not equally strong and the difference is the lesson.

Record one: a screenshot of the composer showing 'Sent successfully', timestamped 10:02. This establishes that the application believed it had handed the message off. It is produced by the system that was hoping.

Record two: the mail provider's API response listing 412 accepted recipients and 3 rejected, with a batch id, timestamped 10:02. This is produced by the system that would know about acceptance. It establishes acceptance - still not delivery.
Record three: a delivery webhook received at 10:09 reporting 406 delivered, 6 bounced. Now delivery is established, for 406 addresses, at that time.

Read together, the honest claim is: 'the newsletter was accepted for 412 addresses and delivered to 406; 3 were rejected at submission and 6 bounced'. Note that nobody has yet established that a single person READ it. Each record extends the claim by exactly one step, and no record extends it further than that.

sections.heading: When this goes wrong
paragraphs: The failure is using record one and reporting the sentence that only record three supports.

'The newsletter went out to all our customers.' Nobody lied. The screenshot is real, the message was real, and the person reporting it saw a success message with their own eyes. But 9 addresses never received it, and the claim covers them.

This gets worse rather than better with time. A month later the screenshot is still in the ledger and the bounce data was never captured, so the gap cannot be reconstructed. Evidence that was weak when recorded does not strengthen; it just gets older and more confidently cited.

The habit worth building is to ask, of every piece of evidence: which system produced this, and what is the next step it does not cover? Then either collect that step or say the claim at the size the evidence actually supports. The second option is available far more often than people use it.

exercise.prompt: Write an evidence note explaining what a receipt proves and what it does not.
checklist: Identify the exact claim being assessed.
Keep a readable source reference.
Record one practical limitation.

check.question: Can a UI success message alone prove external delivery?
choices: Yes, because it is visible.
Yes, if a reviewer clicks complete.
No; external delivery requires its own observable receipt.
check.explanation: Evidence should match the claim. UI state and external delivery are different events.

lessons.legacy_summary: How to review what BuildAndDo observed, decided, attempted, and verified — and what to do when a mission needs attention.

lessons.title: Connecting a self-hosted service
lessons.summary: Read service connection state and prepare a useful operations handoff.
lessons.prerequisites: Read earlier lessons in this path; use an authorized test workspace for exercises.

outcomes: Explain requested, connected and healthy states.
Prepare a connection acceptance check.
lesson.why: A connection request is useful coordination, but confusing it with a running integration can hide the absence of real data.
preparation: Identify a service and an operator authorized to configure it.
Keep host credentials in the private environment.

sections.heading: Understand the idea
paragraphs: Connecting a service means three separate things that people report as one: a credential exists, the credential is accepted, and the credential can do the thing you need. Each can be true without the next, and each fails differently.

PRESENT means a name is set somewhere. USABLE means the far side accepted it and told you who you are. PERMITTED means it may perform the specific operation you want, on the specific object you want. A token that lists your account and cannot read the one project you care about is present, usable and not permitted - and a connection test that stops at the second step will call it healthy.

Read the failure codes rather than the word 'error'. 401 means the credential was rejected: wrong, expired, or revoked. 403 means it was accepted and the action was refused - a different repair entirely. 404 can mean the object does not exist OR that you may not see it, which is why a 404 on something you believe exists is a permission question. And a failure at the edge - a proxy or CDN refusing before your request ever reaches the service - looks like the service saying no and is not.
Scope narrowly on purpose. A credential that can do everything makes every connection succeed and every incident larger. The narrower token that fails loudly on day one is the cheaper one.

One more distinction: a connection that works from your machine and fails from the service is not intermittent. Egress rules, proxies and IP allowlists differ per host, so 'it works locally' and 'it works where it runs' are separate claims and both need testing where the code lives.

sections.heading: Try it in BuildAndDo
steps: For one connected service, find the NAME of the credential in use. Never copy the value - the name is the thing you reason about.
Ask the service who you are (most have a 'current user' or 'whoami' call). Record the identity it returns.
Now ask it to do the narrowest real thing you need, against the actual object. This is the step that distinguishes usable from permitted.
Record the failure code if it fails, not the word 'failed'. Note whether it came from the service or from something in front of it.
Write down what this credential can do that you do NOT need. That list is your blast radius.

sections.heading: Worked example
paragraphs: A workspace needs to read one team's repository activity. Follow what each check establishes.
The environment has a token name set, so it is PRESENT. The whoami call returns an identity, so it is USABLE - at this point most connection tests declare success.

The real request - list commits on project 98 - returns 401. The token was fine a moment ago, so this is not 'the token is broken'. It is a project-scoped token belonging to a different project, and it can authenticate perfectly while being permitted nothing here.

The fix is not a bigger token. Each team has its own scoped credential; using the right one returns 20 commits. The narrow token that failed loudly is what made the mistake visible in a minute rather than a week.

Separately, the same request once returned 403 from a CDN rather than the service, because the client sent a default user agent that the edge blocks. Same URL, same credential, different layer. A 403 that arrives without ever reaching the service is not an authorisation problem.

sections.heading: When this goes wrong
paragraphs: The failure that costs the most is a connection test that stops at 'usable'.

A green tick appears, the integration is declared live, and the first real operation happens days later inside something that matters. By then the 401 arrives in the middle of other work, and because the tick was green nobody suspects the credential.

There is a second, quieter version: the test passes because the credential is enormous. It works on day one and works on everything, so no scope problem is ever discovered - until an incident, when the answer to 'what could this have touched' is 'all of it'.
Test the narrow thing you actually need, against the real object, and record the code you got. 'It connected' is not a result you can act on later.

exercise.prompt: Prepare an operations note for one service connection without including a secret.
checklist: Name the operator and intended environment.
Describe a minimal non-production check.
Separate configuration completion from useful-operation health.

check.question: A service shows Pending. What is established?
choices: A connection has been requested or is awaiting completion.
The service is healthy.
All its data has synchronized.
check.explanation: Pending is coordination state. Health and synchronization need later observations.

lessons.legacy_summary: What the Operations area means, the planned self-hosted stack, and how connection status works.

lessons.title: Define a measurable business objective
lessons.summary: Turn a broad ambition into an ERP objective with a useful success measure and review date.
lessons.prerequisites: Read earlier lessons in this path; use an authorized test workspace for exercises.

outcomes: Describe a baseline, target and observation period.
Save and edit an ERP objective.
lesson.why: A measurable objective helps people decide which tasks matter and when the work is sufficient. The measure should reflect a business result rather than the number of buttons clicked.
preparation: Choose one process you understand.
Use an observed baseline or explicitly mark it as unknown.

sections.heading: Understand the idea
paragraphs: An objective is measurable when somebody who disagrees with you could still check it. That is a higher bar than having a number in the sentence, and a much more useful one.

Three things make the difference. A SOURCE somebody else can read. A THRESHOLD stated before the measurement, not chosen afterwards. And a WINDOW, so the same question asked twice gets a comparable answer. Remove any one and you have a direction of travel rather than an objective.

The most common failure is an objective whose measurement does not exist yet. 'Improve onboarding completion' assumes something records completion. If it does not, the first piece of work is building the measurement, and pretending otherwise means the objective will be assessed on impressions at the end.
State what would falsify it. An objective that cannot come out false is a statement of intent wearing a number.

sections.heading: Try it in BuildAndDo
steps: Take one objective you are carrying and write down the source that would measure it, by name.
If no source exists, stop - the real first task is creating one. Write that down as the objective instead.
Write the threshold and the window explicitly: what value, measured over what period.
Take the measurement NOW and record it as the baseline, before any work starts.
Write the sentence that would be true if the objective failed. If you cannot, it is not yet measurable.

sections.heading: Worked example
paragraphs: A curriculum team wants lessons that are worth a reader's time. Watch it become checkable.
First attempt: 'make the lessons better'. No source, no threshold, no window. Nobody could disagree with it, which feels like agreement and is not.

The measurement is invented deliberately: instructional words divided by the minutes each lesson claims from a reader. It is crude, and crucially it is stated so it can be argued with. The threshold is 60 words per claimed minute; below that a lesson is asking for more time than it gives back.
Baseline, taken before any writing: 33 lessons, 9,619 instructional words against 467 declared minutes - 20.6 per claimed minute, and zero lessons above the floor.

After the first five lessons were rewritten: 12,292 words, 26.3 per claimed minute, five lessons above the floor. Both numbers come from the same source and the same script, so the comparison means something. Note the objective could have failed: if the rewrite had added words without clearing 60, the measurement would have said so.

sections.heading: When this goes wrong
paragraphs: The characteristic failure is choosing the threshold after seeing the result.

Suppose the rewrite had reached 45 words per claimed minute, and somebody had then said 'well, 45 is really fine for a short lesson'. Everything about the process looks identical - a source, a number, a comparison - and nothing is being tested. The threshold has become a description of whatever happened.

A related version: quietly reducing the claim instead of doing the work. One lesson here measured 53.9 against the 60 floor. Editing its declared minutes from 14 down to 12 would have cleared the floor instantly, satisfied the check, and cheated the reader, who is still getting the same thin lesson.
Write the threshold down before you measure, and when you miss it, say you missed it. The number is only worth having because it can embarrass you.

There is a third version worth naming because it is the most respectable-looking. The measurement is real, the threshold was fixed in advance, and the source quietly changes underneath - a filter is added, a date range shifts, a field is renamed and back-filled. The before and after are then two different questions with one label, and the comparison is meaningless in a way no one can see from the numbers. Pin the source: same script, same parameters, and record them beside the result.

exercise.prompt: Create or sketch one objective whose result a second person could assess.
checklist: Separate the intended result from an action.
Identify a source for the measure.
Keep unknown baseline values explicitly unknown.

check.question: Which is the stronger success measure?
choices: Make the process better.
Use the dashboard every day.
Reduce median response time from an observed baseline to a named target over a defined period.
check.explanation: The last measure defines an assessable outcome. Activity alone does not establish improvement.

lessons.title: Break an objective into linked tasks
lessons.summary: Create small ERP tasks that remain connected to the objective they support.
lessons.prerequisites: Read earlier lessons in this path; use an authorized test workspace for exercises.

outcomes: Save a task with a clear completion condition.
Link it to the correct workspace objective and contact.
lesson.why: A task list becomes easier to prioritize when each action has a visible purpose. Linking a task to an objective preserves that context during handoffs.
preparation: Have one saved objective.
Add a test contact only if you have permission to store the information.

sections.heading: Understand the idea
paragraphs: Decomposition is not chopping an objective into smaller descriptions of the same objective. It is finding the pieces that can be finished, checked, and handed to someone else independently.

A good task has an owner, an end state somebody else can confirm, and no hidden dependency on a task nobody has written down. The last one causes most of the trouble: work stalls not because a task was hard but because it was waiting on something that existed only in somebody's head.

Sequence by what unblocks the most, not by what is easiest. And put the task that could invalidate the whole objective FIRST - if the measurement turns out to be unbuildable, you want to know in week one, not after four weeks of work that assumed it.

sections.heading: Try it in BuildAndDo
steps: Write the objective's end state as one sentence somebody else could verify.
List every piece of work that has to be true for that sentence to hold.
For each piece, name an owner and what 'done' looks like to a person who did not do it.
Mark which pieces depend on which. Any dependency you cannot name a task for is a missing task.
Identify the piece that could prove the objective impossible, and put it first.

sections.heading: Worked example
paragraphs: Objective: the five first-path lessons clear the depth floor. Decompose it.

Piece one, and it goes first because it could invalidate everything: can depth be measured at all? If instructional words cannot be extracted from the lesson structure, there is no objective here. Done means a script prints a number for every lesson.
Piece two: baseline every lesson and identify which are below the floor. Done means a list with five slugs and their current figures.
Piece three: rewrite each lesson. Done means a worked example with real numbers and a failure case exist in the content.

Piece four: get the rewrite onto the live service without taking it down. This depends on piece three and on a preflight existing - which was a task in a different guild's work, and naming that dependency is what stopped it being a surprise.
Piece five: re-measure with the same script from piece one. Done means the comparison is against the same source, which is the only reason it means anything.

sections.heading: When this goes wrong
paragraphs: The usual failure is a task list that is really one task written five times.

'Review lessons, improve lessons, polish lessons, check lessons, finalise lessons' has five rows and one piece of work. Nothing can be handed over, nothing can be finished, and progress can only be reported as a feeling.

The other failure is discovering the invalidating piece last. If depth had turned out to be unmeasurable from the lesson structure, finding that out after writing five lessons would have wasted the writing - not because the writing was bad, but because nobody could have shown it helped.
Ask of each task: could a colleague finish this and tell me it is done, without me explaining what I meant? If not, it is a heading rather than a task.

exercise.prompt: Break one objective into three tasks with different observable outputs.
checklist: Link each task to the objective.
Make each output reviewable.
Keep customer outreach outside the exercise unless separately authorized.

check.question: Does choosing a contact grant that person workspace access?
choices: Yes, contacts are workspace members.
No; contact records and account permissions are separate.
Only when the task is high priority.
check.explanation: Contact linking describes coordination. Workspace membership remains the authentication and role system’s responsibility.

lessons.title: Prioritize tasks and review due dates
lessons.summary: Use explicit status, priority and overdue views to decide the next useful action.
lessons.prerequisites: Read earlier lessons in this path; use an authorized test workspace for exercises.

outcomes: Filter open and overdue work.
Change task state deliberately without losing the plan.
lesson.why: Dates and priorities are useful when they support decisions. Marking everything urgent hides real constraints and makes missed commitments harder to see.
preparation: Use at least two authorized test tasks or the worked example.
Choose dates according to your local calendar.

sections.heading: Understand the idea
paragraphs: Priority is a statement about what you will NOT do. A list where everything is high has not prioritised anything; it has recorded that everything felt important on the day it was written.

Dates carry a claim too, and it is worth being explicit about which kind. A date can be a CONSTRAINT that exists outside you - a submission deadline, a certificate expiry, a contract date. Or it can be an ESTIMATE, which is a guess with a confidence attached. Writing both in the same field means nobody can tell which are real.

When a constraint is close, priority stops being about value and becomes about what is reachable. The right question shifts from 'what is most important' to 'what can be finished and proved before the date', and those have different answers.

sections.heading: Try it in BuildAndDo
steps: Take your current list and mark each date as CONSTRAINT or ESTIMATE. Note how many you cannot classify.
For each constraint, write what actually happens if it is missed. Some turn out to have no consequence at all.
Force a ranking with no ties. If two items are equal, ask which you would drop first under pressure.
Write down what the bottom three items are NOT getting done in favour of.
For anything before a near constraint, ask whether it can be finished AND demonstrated in time, not just started.

sections.heading: Worked example
paragraphs: Three days before a submission deadline, a team holds eight open items. Work the ranking.
The deadline is a CONSTRAINT: it is set by somebody else and missing it means not being considered. Everything else on the list carries estimates.

Two items are half-built features. Both are valuable and neither can be finished and demonstrated in three days. Under a near constraint they drop, not because they stopped mattering but because an unfinished feature demonstrates nothing.
One item is a broken link on the page a reviewer opens first. It is small, dull, and it is now top of the list - its value is not its size, it is its position relative to the constraint.
The ranking that results is not the ranking anyone would have written a month earlier, and that is correct. The list did not change; the distance to the constraint did.

sections.heading: When this goes wrong
paragraphs: The failure is a list where every item is high priority and every date is 'this sprint'.

It feels rigorous - there are dates, there are priorities - and it makes no decision. When the week runs short, what actually gets dropped is whatever was least fresh in someone's mind, and nobody agreed to that.

The second failure is mistaking an estimate for a constraint. A team treats an internal target as immovable, ships something unfinished to hit it, and discovers the date had no consequence attached. The cost was real and the deadline was not.
Before defending a date, answer plainly: who set it, and what happens if it slips? If the answer is 'we did' and 'nothing', it is an estimate, and it should not be costing you scope.

exercise.prompt: Prepare a three-item next-action list using priority, due dates and dependency judgment.
checklist: Give each priority a reason.
Exclude completed work from overdue action items.
Record a next review date for unscheduled work.

check.question: How should a missing due date be treated?
choices: As unscheduled work.
As the Unix epoch.
As automatically due today.
check.explanation: A missing value is unknown or unscheduled. Inventing a date distorts the planning view.

lessons.title: Keep useful, minimal contact records
lessons.summary: Maintain contact context without turning notes into a store for unnecessary personal data.
lessons.prerequisites: Read earlier lessons in this path; use an authorized test workspace for exercises.

outcomes: Create and edit a purpose-limited contact.
Separate notes, authority and actual outreach.
lesson.why: Useful contact records make coordination easier. Collecting more personal data than the task needs increases both confusion and exposure.
preparation: Use a consenting colleague or synthetic example.
Know why this workspace needs the record.

sections.heading: Understand the idea
paragraphs: Contact data decays whether or not anyone touches it. People change jobs, domains lapse, numbers get reassigned. A record that was correct when captured is not a record that is correct now, and nothing about storing it more neatly changes that.

Keep three facts about every contact: where it came from, when it was last CONFIRMED, and whether the person agreed to be contacted. Confirmed is not the same as captured - captured is when it entered your system, confirmed is the last time something outside your system agreed it was still true.

Bounces and complaints are measurements, not annoyances. A rising bounce rate is your list telling you its age. Sending harder into a decaying list damages the delivery of messages to the addresses that still work, so the cost is not limited to the bad rows.

Deleting a stale record is usually the right answer and usually feels like a loss. A list of 1,000 addresses where 400 are dead is not bigger than a list of 600; it is a list of 600 with worse deliverability and a misleading number on it.

sections.heading: Try it in BuildAndDo
steps: Pick 20 contacts at random and find, for each, the source and the date it was last confirmed.
Count how many you cannot answer for. That proportion is your real data quality figure.
Find your bounce and complaint rates for the last send. If you cannot, that is the finding.
Identify records with no confirmation in over a year and decide explicitly: re-confirm or remove. Leaving them is also a decision, so make it deliberately.
Write down the one habit that would have kept these current, and whether anything enforces it.

sections.heading: Worked example
paragraphs: A list of 1,240 addresses is used for a monthly update. Work the numbers.
Last send: 1,240 attempted, 1,112 accepted, 128 hard bounces. That is 10.3% - high enough that mailbox providers begin treating the sender with suspicion, which affects the 1,112 as well.
Sampling 20 records for provenance: 6 have a source and a confirmation date, 9 have a source only, 5 have neither. So roughly a quarter of the list cannot be accounted for at all.
The 128 bouncing addresses are removed - the list is now 1,112 and is honestly larger than it was, because the number now describes reachable people.

The 5-in-20 with no provenance are a different problem and cannot be fixed by cleaning. They get a re-confirmation message; those who do not respond are removed. A contact you cannot say you acquired lawfully is a liability, not an asset.

sections.heading: When this goes wrong
paragraphs: The failure is treating list size as the metric.

A team reports 1,240 contacts and next month 1,300. The number goes up, everyone is pleased, and the bounce rate is not in the report. Six months later delivery has degraded for everyone, including the customers who do want to hear from them.

The compounding version: because the bad addresses were never removed, the sender reputation drops, which reduces delivery to good addresses, which reduces engagement, which reduces delivery further. Nothing in the contact list looks wrong at any point.
Report reachable contacts and bounce rate together, always. A contact count on its own is a measure of how long you have been collecting, not of how many people you can reach.

exercise.prompt: Review a contact note and remove information that is unnecessary for its purpose.
checklist: State the reason for storing the contact.
Exclude secrets and sensitive personal detail.
Identify when the record should be reviewed or removed.

check.question: What does saving an email address do?
choices: Subscribe the person to a campaign.
Grant permission to email them.
Store a contact field; outreach and permission are separate.
check.explanation: Storage is not consent or delivery. Keep those decisions explicit.

lessons.title: Scope risk and plan recovery
lessons.summary: Write a bounded risk assessment and a rollback that preserves useful records.
lessons.prerequisites: Read earlier lessons in this path; use an authorized test workspace for exercises.

outcomes: Identify affected users, data and systems.
Define stop conditions and a recovery check.
lesson.why: Recovery is easier to design before a failure. A rollback plan should identify the state you intend to restore and the evidence you must retain.
preparation: Choose a small proposed change.
Know the environment and authority for that change.

sections.heading: Understand the idea
paragraphs: A rollback plan is not a promise that you can undo something. It is a written answer to three questions asked before you start: what does this touch, how would I know it went wrong, and what is the fastest way back to a known state.
The most important of those is the middle one. Plenty of changes are reversible and still cause damage, because nobody noticed for a week. A rollback you cannot trigger is not a rollback.

Know which changes are genuinely irreversible: deleted data with no backup, messages sent to real people, money moved, credentials published. For those, the rollback plan is really a REHEARSAL plan - you prove it on a copy, because there is no second chance on the original.
'Restore from backup' is only a plan if the backup exists, is recent, and has been restored at least once. An untested backup is a belief.

Distinguish the rollback from the recovery. A rollback returns the system to its previous state; a recovery returns the BUSINESS to a working position, and those are not always the same action. If a bad export sent wrong figures to a customer, reverting the export changes nothing about what they received, and the recovery is a correction they can see.

sections.heading: Try it in BuildAndDo
steps: Write down every system this change touches, including the ones you touch only by restarting them.
Write the signal you would see within minutes if it went wrong, and say who would see it.
Write the path back: the exact command or action, and how long it takes.
Take the backup BEFORE the change and note its name. A backup taken after is a copy of the problem.
For anything irreversible, rehearse on a copy first and record what the rehearsal showed.

sections.heading: Worked example
paragraphs: Twelve database migrations need to reach a live backend. Walk the risk.

What it touches: the schema, and therefore the whole service. On this backend a failed migration does not fail the migration - it aborts startup, so the blast radius is the entire API, not the one table.
How you would know: the service does not come up. That is a fast, unambiguous signal, which is the good case - the dangerous changes are the ones with no signal.
Path back: restore the database file and restart. Time: about two minutes, IF a copy exists.
The copy was taken first, named data.db.pre-migration with the date. When the set did take the service down, recovery was two minutes of a known procedure rather than an incident.

The rehearsal step came later and is the real lesson: applying the same set to a COPY first would have shown the failure without any downtime at all. A rollback that works is good; not needing it is better.

One detail from that incident is worth keeping. The service came back in two minutes, and the team's first instinct was to call the rollback plan a success. It was, and it was also the second-best outcome available: the same set applied to a copy beforehand would have produced the same information with no downtime at all. A rollback you had to use is a lesson about the step before it.

sections.heading: When this goes wrong
paragraphs: The failure is a rollback plan written as a sentence in a ticket: 'revert if there are issues'.

It names no backup, no signal and no command. In the moment, with the service down, somebody is improvising under pressure - and the first thing they reach for is often the thing that makes recovery harder, like restarting repeatedly or re-running the change.
The specific trap worth naming: taking the backup as part of the deploy, after the change has begun. It feels like diligence. It captures the broken state.
If the plan does not name a file, a command and a time, it is not a plan. Write it while calm, because you will read it while not.

One more pattern, and it is the one that turns a small problem into an outage: rolling back under pressure without recording what state you were in. Half the change is reverted, a service is restarted twice, and afterwards nobody can say which version is running or which migrations applied. The incident is over and the system is now in a state nobody designed. Write down what you did as you do it, even in the middle - especially in the middle.

exercise.prompt: Write a four-line risk and recovery note for one ERP or content change.
checklist: Bound the environment and affected data.
Define a measurable stop condition.
Preserve records needed to understand the failure.

check.question: Which is a useful recovery check?
choices: The rollback command printed no error.
The previous accepted behavior is observed and retained data remains readable.
Someone said the system looks fine.
check.explanation: A command outcome is only one part of recovery. Verify the behavior and data you intended to restore.

lessons.title: Design four distinct TEVV checks
lessons.summary: Use testing, evaluation, verification and validation to gather different kinds of evidence.
lessons.prerequisites: Read earlier lessons in this path; use an authorized test workspace for exercises.

outcomes: Distinguish the four TEVV activities.
Connect each method to a claim and an observation.
lesson.why: A single passing test rarely answers every question about a system. Distinct checks make gaps visible before a team claims the work is successful.
preparation: Use a bounded mission with a success criterion.
Read the linked NIST guidance as context, not as a certification checklist.

sections.heading: Understand the idea
paragraphs: TEVV is test, evaluate, verify and validate, and the four words are not synonyms for checking. TEST asks whether it behaves as specified. EVALUATE asks how well, against a threshold set beforehand. VERIFY asks whether we built the thing correctly. VALIDATE asks the harder question: whether the thing we built was the right thing at all.

A check that has only ever passed has not been tested. This is the single most useful idea in the practice: a checker that agrees with you every time might be measuring the system, or it might be reflecting you, and from the output those look identical.
So every check needs a case it REFUSES, demonstrated. Not described - demonstrated, with the refusal recorded next to the pass. The red is what gives the green meaning.
Design the evaluation before you run it. A threshold chosen after seeing the result is a description of the result, and an evaluation that cannot come out negative is not measuring anything.

Sequence matters. Run the negative control BEFORE the real measurement, not after it. Once you have a green result in hand, every instinct pushes toward accepting it, and a control run afterwards is answering a question you have already decided.

Separate the four activities across people where you can. The person who built a thing is the worst-placed to verify it and the best-placed to test it, because they know where it is fragile. Validation in particular benefits from somebody who does not know how it works and does know what it was for.

sections.heading: Try it in BuildAndDo
steps: For one check you rely on, write what it would look like if the check itself were broken.
Construct an input it must refuse. Run it. Record the refusal.
If it does not refuse, you have learned something more valuable than a pass - the check was not testing what you thought.
Write the evaluation threshold down before the next run.
Ask the validate question once: if this check passes forever, is the underlying thing actually good? Note what it does not cover.

sections.heading: Worked example
paragraphs: A content checker reports that all 33 lessons are broken. Work it as TEVV rather than reacting.
TEST: does it behave as specified? It runs, it produces findings in the right shape, it exits cleanly. It passes this and the finding is still false.

VERIFY - did we build it correctly? Three defects, each of which produced a finding rather than an error: a fetch truncated to 4,000 bytes, so a 761KB bundle was searched over its first 4KB and no routes were found; a patched pattern carried an invisible control byte, so a filter that read as correct never matched; and prerequisites were compared against a graph the curriculum does not have.

The negative control is what settled it. Feed the checker a link that is genuinely broken and a link that is genuinely fine: if both come back broken, the checker is the problem. That single run would have caught all three defects on day one.

VALIDATE: even once correct, the checker says every lesson passes structurally. Is that the right thing to measure? No - it says nothing about whether a lesson teaches, which is why a second measure of depth was needed. A perfect score on the wrong question is still a wrong answer.

It is worth noticing how the three defects were alike. Each was in the measuring apparatus, each produced output in the shape of a real finding, and none raised an error. That is the signature of instrument failure, and it is why TEVV puts verify and validate as separate questions - the tool was correct by its own specification and wrong about the world.

The cost of not running a control is not the bad finding. It is the remediation work that follows: had the first report been believed, somebody would have spent a week repairing 33 lessons that were not broken, and the repair would have looked successful, because the checker would have gone on reporting whatever it reported.

sections.heading: When this goes wrong
paragraphs: The failure is treating a green result as evidence when the checker has never been seen to go red.
It is worse than no check, because it is a receipt. Somebody later reads 'verified' and does not re-examine, and the unexamined assumption travels further than it would have without the ceremony.

The version that costs most is a check that passes because it could not look - an empty match, an unreachable path, a permission error swallowed. Zero problems found and zero things examined produce the same output, and only one of them is good news.
Make every check answer two questions: what did you examine, and what would you have refused? A check that cannot answer the second is decoration with a exit code.

A quieter failure: evaluating against a threshold that was never written down, so the evaluation becomes a conversation about whether the number feels acceptable. Everybody argues in good faith and the answer depends on who is in the room and how the week has gone. Writing the threshold down is not bureaucracy - it is the only thing that makes the result independent of the mood.

And the failure that looks most like diligence: running many checks, none of which has a control. Ten green results are not ten pieces of evidence if none of the ten has ever been shown to go red. They are one unexamined assumption, repeated.

Finally, be wary of the word 'verified' in a status field. It records that somebody ran something, not that the something could have failed. When you read it on work you did not do, the useful question is never whether it passed - it is what the check would have refused, and whether anyone ever saw it refuse anything.

exercise.prompt: Create four different TEVV methods for the same small content workflow.
checklist: Name the claim each method addresses.
Specify an observable artifact.
State what remains untested or uncertain.

check.question: Which activity most directly asks whether the result serves the intended user?
choices: Validation.
Counting source files.
Checking whether a command exists.
check.explanation: Validation addresses intended use. File counts and command availability do not establish user value.

lessons.title: Apply practical OWASP checks
lessons.summary: Check authorization, input handling and data exposure at the boundary where the operation happens.
lessons.prerequisites: Read earlier lessons in this path; use an authorized test workspace for exercises.

outcomes: Identify a cross-workspace test case.
Explain why content should render as text rather than executable HTML.
lesson.why: A disabled button is helpful guidance, but it cannot protect a backend from direct requests. Security checks belong at the actual authorization boundary.
preparation: Use isolated test accounts and workspaces only.
Obtain authorization before exercising any security test.

sections.heading: Understand the idea
paragraphs: Most workspace security failures are not exotic. They are authorisation mistakes: the system correctly works out WHO you are and then fails to check WHAT you may touch. Authentication is usually solid because it is visible; authorisation fails quietly because it only shows up when someone crosses a boundary nobody tested.

The pattern to look for is a rule that checks a user is logged in and then trusts a field in the request to decide scope. If the request says which workspace to write into, and the rule only confirms you are somebody, then anybody can write anywhere.

Rules are code and can be wrong in ways that read as correct. A guard comparing a rule to a string can be comparing two different types and silently never match - so the guard is present, looks careful, and never fires.
Test authorisation from the other side. The question is not 'can the owner do this', it is 'can a member of a different workspace do this', and the only way to know is to try it as them.

The same shape appears in reads. A list endpoint that filters by a field the caller supplies will happily list another workspace's records if asked nicely, and it does not feel like a breach because nothing was written. Data leaving is as serious as data arriving.

Anonymous access needs its own test, and the result is easy to misread. A collection that returns an empty list to a stranger may be correctly refusing, or it may be returning everything a stranger is allowed to see, which happens to be nothing today and something tomorrow. An empty result is not the same as a refusal, and only one of them is a boundary.

sections.heading: Try it in BuildAndDo
steps: Pick one collection users can write to. Read its create rule out loud in plain language.
Ask: does anything in that rule tie the new record to a workspace the caller belongs to?
Try the write as a user from a DIFFERENT workspace. Expect a refusal; treat a success as a finding.
Check any guard that compares values, and confirm the two sides are the same type.
Write down which collections you have tested from the outside, and which you have only assumed.

sections.heading: Worked example
paragraphs: A workspace collection carried this create rule: the caller is authenticated, and the owner field in the request equals the caller's id. Work out what it permits.
It reads as careful. It names the caller, it checks a field matches them, and it refuses anonymous writes. Every part of it is doing something.

What it never does is check the WORKSPACE. Any authenticated user, setting owner to their own id, could create a record inside any workspace at all - by naming it in the request. The rule confirms who you are and takes your word for where.

Two migrations existed to replace that rule with one that checks membership. Neither had ever applied, because each guarded itself by comparing the stored rule to a string - and on this runtime rules are objects, so the comparison was always false and the guard always skipped. The hole stayed open for five days behind two fixes that looked applied.
It was found by trying the write as a member of another workspace, which took under a minute. Nothing in reading the rule would have revealed the type problem.

The cheap habit that catches this class of defect: keep a second account in a second workspace, and make every authorisation change end with one attempt from it. It takes a minute, it needs no tooling, and it tests the thing the rule text cannot tell you - what the system does when somebody who should be refused actually asks.

sections.heading: When this goes wrong
paragraphs: The failure is auditing authorisation by reading rules instead of exercising them.
Reading tells you what somebody intended. Exercising tells you what the system does. In this case the intention was correct and present in the repository twice, and the behaviour was wide open.
A related failure is testing only the happy path - the owner can write to their own workspace, so authorisation works. That test passes identically whether or not the boundary exists.
For every rule you care about, have one recorded attempt from the wrong side that was refused. That refusal is the evidence the boundary is real; the rule text is only the claim.

The aftermath is worth understanding too. When a boundary is found open, the first question is not how to close it but what went through it. Without records of who wrote what into which workspace, the honest answer is that you cannot tell - so the fix is urgent and the investigation is impossible, which is the worst combination. Authorisation logging is what makes an open boundary a bounded incident rather than an unbounded one.
Treat every authorisation rule as unproven until a refusal from the wrong side has been recorded against it. The rule text is a claim; the refusal is the evidence.

exercise.prompt: Add three boundary checks to a mission plan without probing any unapproved system.
checklist: Test the backend boundary, not only the UI.
Use synthetic records.
Document failed or unavailable checks honestly.

check.question: Where must a same-workspace relation be enforced?
choices: Only in the dropdown.
Only in a tutorial.
In the server request policy as well as the UI.
check.explanation: Clients can be bypassed. The server must validate the actual linked record and current caller permissions.

lessons.title: Build a workflow with an approval checkpoint
lessons.summary: Save a reusable procedure and record its ordered steps with an explicit approval decision.
lessons.prerequisites: Read earlier lessons in this path; use an authorized test workspace for exercises.

outcomes: Separate workflow activation from a recorded run.
Use an approval checkpoint before a consequential step.
lesson.why: A reusable definition makes repeat work consistent. A separate run history preserves what was actually recorded for a particular attempt.
preparation: Use an authorized test workspace with the workflow backend installed.
Have an owner or admin available for an approval exercise.

sections.heading: Understand the idea
paragraphs: An approval checkpoint exists so that a decision has a place to happen and a record of having happened. Its value is entirely in the possibility of NO. A checkpoint that always approves has the cost of a gate and the effect of a comment.

Put the checkpoint before the irreversible step, not after the work. Approving something that is already done is a formality; approving something about to send messages, spend money, or change a live system is a decision.

The approver needs enough to decide and not so much that they cannot. That means the claim, the evidence behind it, and what happens if it is wrong - not the full history. If your approval request cannot be read in two minutes it will be approved without being read.
Record who approved, when, and what they saw. The last part matters most: an approval of a changed scope is not an approval of the current one, so a material change re-opens the gate.

An approver needs standing as well as information. Asking someone to approve work they cannot refuse - because of seniority, or because the work is already done, or because the deadline passed this morning - produces a signature and no decision. If the answer can only be yes, move the checkpoint earlier rather than pretending.

Distinguish approving the DECISION from approving the EXECUTION. Agreeing that a thing should be done is not agreeing that this particular attempt, with this scope and this blast radius, should run now. Many workflows need both, and collapsing them means the second never happens.

sections.heading: Try it in BuildAndDo
steps: Find one workflow you run and mark the first genuinely irreversible step.
Check whether an approval exists before it. If it is after, the gate is decorative.
Write what the approver sees. Include the evidence and the failure case, not just the request.
Ask when someone last declined at this checkpoint. If never, ask whether it could happen.
Confirm that changing the scope after approval re-opens the gate rather than inheriting it.

sections.heading: Worked example
paragraphs: Eight pieces of work are proposed, one per team, each with the evidence for why it matters. Watch the checkpoint do its job.
Each team is asked to accept or decline its own item, and told explicitly that declining is a legitimate answer. Seven accept with reasons that cite the evidence they were given.

All accepting is exactly the pattern that should not be trusted, so a control is run: one team is offered an item that plainly belongs to another team. It declines, correctly naming the owner. The checkpoint discriminates, and only now do the seven acceptances mean something.

The mechanism also refuses on silence. When a team could not be reached, its item stayed proposed rather than defaulting to approved - because an approval that happens when nobody answers is not an approval.
One item was moved between teams and put to the new owner as a fresh decision rather than inheriting the previous acceptance. The work did not change; the person answering for it did.

Notice what made the control meaningful: it was run BEFORE the acceptances were acted on, not afterwards as reassurance. A gate validated after its decisions have been implemented is collecting comfort rather than evidence.

The wider point is that unanimity is information. Seven acceptances told us very little on their own; the same seven, alongside one demonstrated refusal, told us the gate distinguishes. Treat a 100% approval rate as a question rather than a result.

sections.heading: When this goes wrong
paragraphs: The failure is the checkpoint that cannot say no.

The commonest form is self-approval at the moment of writing: propose, approve, start, all in one action. Every field is filled and the audit trail is complete. No scope was ever accepted, because none was offered to anyone.
The subtler form is approval by timeout - if nobody objects in two days it proceeds. That is not consent, it is absence, and it will eventually record an approval from someone who was on holiday.
Two tests. Has anyone ever declined here? And what happens if the approver simply does not answer - does the work stop, or does it proceed with a receipt saying it was approved?

There is also the checkpoint that is technically refusable and practically not, because declining costs the approver more than approving. If saying no means a week of argument and saying yes means moving on, the gate will trend toward yes regardless of the merits - and it will look like consensus. Notice when your approval rate is 100% and ask whether that reflects the work or the cost of objecting.

A last check worth running on your own process: pick the most consequential gate you have and find the last time it changed an outcome. If the answer is that it never has, you are paying the cost of a gate - the delay, the ceremony, the coordination - and receiving none of its benefit, and it would be more honest to remove it than to keep signing.

exercise.prompt: Record one approved checkpoint and inspect the run snapshot.
checklist: Keep each decision in the original step order.
Identify the saved approval actor and time.
Do not claim external tool execution from a recorded step.

check.question: What does activating a workflow prove?
choices: All its steps ran.
The definition is available to start; it does not prove an execution.
An external message was sent.
check.explanation: Definition state and execution history are separate. A real run begins with the start command.

lessons.title: Review a failed run and retry safely
lessons.summary: Preserve observations after failure and avoid creating duplicate evidence when a response is uncertain.
lessons.prerequisites: Read earlier lessons in this path; use an authorized test workspace for exercises.

outcomes: Distinguish a rejected operation from a lost response.
Explain why terminal runs are retained.
lesson.why: A failed attempt can teach as much as a passing one if the record is preserved. Retrying carelessly can turn a recoverable network problem into duplicate work.
preparation: Use a test workflow and synthetic observations.
Do not cause failures in a shared production service.

sections.heading: Understand the idea
paragraphs: A retry is safe when repeating the operation produces the same result as doing it once. That property is called idempotency, and without it a retry is a second attempt at a thing that may already have happened.

The dangerous case is not a failure - it is an UNKNOWN. The request timed out. You do not know whether the far side processed it. Retrying might duplicate a payment or a message; not retrying might drop it. The only way out is to make the question answerable in advance, with a key the far side remembers.

Send an idempotency key with the operation and have the receiver record it. A repeat carrying the same key returns the original result rather than acting again. The key must describe the INTENT - same key for the same intended operation - or a retry becomes a new operation wearing the same name.

Distinguish the failures. A 4xx usually means retrying will fail identically; fix the request. A 5xx or a timeout may be transient. Retrying a 4xx forever is how a queue fills with work that can never succeed.

Bound your retries and back off between them. Immediate, unlimited retries turn a brief wobble on the far side into a sustained load that prevents it recovering - your client becomes the reason the outage continues. Exponential spacing with a ceiling, and a limit after which the work goes somewhere a human will see it.

Decide what happens to work that exhausts its retries. Dropping it silently is a decision, just not a recorded one. A dead-letter destination turns an invisible loss into a visible queue, and the queue is the honest state.

sections.heading: Try it in BuildAndDo
steps: For one operation you retry, decide whether repeating it twice would be harmless. Write the answer down.
If it would not, find or add an idempotency key, and make it a function of the intent rather than the attempt.
Deliberately send the same operation twice and confirm the second returns the first result rather than acting again.
Now change one field and send it with the same key. A good receiver refuses this - the key promised the same intent.
Separate your retryable failures from your permanent ones and check what your system does with each.

sections.heading: Worked example
paragraphs: A step in a run is recorded twice - once because a connection dropped mid-request. Follow what the key does.
The first attempt carries a key derived from the intent: the run, the step, and the day. It succeeds, and the receiver stores the key with the result.
The connection drops before the response arrives. The caller does not know whether it worked, which is the genuinely hard case - both retrying and not retrying can be wrong.
It retries with the same key. The receiver recognises the key and returns the original receipt without recording a second step. The uncertainty is resolved without a duplicate.

Later the same key is sent with different content, and the receiver refuses: 'this request key already belongs to a different decision.' That refusal is the mechanism working. The key means 'this exact intent'; reusing it for another one would let a retry silently overwrite a decision, and a 409 there is more useful than a success.

The 409 is worth sitting with, because it feels like a failure and is the system protecting you. The alternative - accepting a reused key with different content - would let a retry silently replace a recorded decision with a different one, and nothing downstream would ever know which had been kept. An error you can read beats a success you cannot trust.

sections.heading: When this goes wrong
paragraphs: The failure is a retry loop with a fresh key on every attempt.
It looks like a retry and behaves like a queue of new work. Three timeouts produce three operations, each believing it is the first. For a message that is three sends; for a payment it is worse.

The other failure is retrying what cannot succeed. A request rejected for a malformed field will be rejected identically forever, and a loop that treats every failure as transient turns one bad request into unbounded load - and hides the real error inside thousands of copies of itself.
Before writing a retry, answer two questions: is this operation safe to repeat, and which failures am I retrying? A retry without both answers is an amplifier.
